questions.prompt: Which file descriptors are open by default in every process?
options: None: the program must open them
questions.explain: By convention 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, standard output and standard error. The shell sets them up before your program starts.

questions.prompt: A process closes descriptor 0 and then successfully calls `open` on a file. What does `open` return?
questions.explain: `open` (and `dup`) return the LOWEST unused descriptor of the process. After `close(0)` that is 0, so the file silently becomes the program's standard input.
option_notes: 3 is only the lowest free number if 0, 1 and 2 are open.

questions.explain: `creat` creates the file if needed, empties it if it exists, and opens it write-only.
option_notes: Opens read-only and does not truncate.
That opens read-write and appends instead of truncating.
Without O_CREAT the file is not created and the mode is ignored.

questions.prompt: What is true after `int fd2 = dup(fd1);`?
options: fd1 and fd2 share the same file offset
fd2 is the lowest unused descriptor number
Writing through fd2 changes the offset seen through fd1
questions.explain: Both descriptors refer to the same open file, so they share the offset and flags. They are closed independently, and the file stays open until both are closed.
option_notes: False: each descriptor is closed on its own.
True: dup picks the lowest free number.

questions.prompt: Opening the same file twice with `open` gives two descriptors with {{0}} file offsets (shared or independent?).
questions.explain: Each `open` creates a new open file description with its own offset. Only `dup`/`dup2` (and `fork`) share one.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of copying a file with system calls in order.
items: Open the source file with open(O_RDONLY)
Loop: read a chunk and write the bytes you got, until read returns 0
questions.explain: Always write exactly as many bytes as `read` returned (not the buffer size), stop when `read` returns 0 (end of file) and release both descriptors.
